title: Renting a Car in Korea: International Driving Permit Rules, Costs, and Driving Tips for First-Timers
html:
Public transport in Korea is good enough that most visitors never need to drive. But if your trip includes Jeju Island, a coastal road trip, or small countryside temples and villages that buses only reach a few times a day, renting a car can save you hours. The catch: Korea has a few paperwork and driving-rule quirks that trip up first-timers. Here's what you actually need to know before you book.

The Paperwork: International Driving Permit, Age Rules, and What It Costs

To rent a car in Korea, you need a physical International Driving Permit (IDP) — not a digital copy, not a photo on your phone. Korean rental companies almost always ask for an IDP issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention; permits from countries that only issue a Vienna-style (1968) version, or no IDP at all (this includes a handful of countries, so check your own), may not be accepted. Get your IDP before you leave home — it's issued by your own country's motoring authority (for example, AAA or AATA in the US), and you cannot apply for one once you're already in Korea.

Along with the IDP, bring your passport, your physical home driver's license (the IDP is only valid together with it, not on its own), and a credit card in the name of whoever is driving. Most companies require drivers to be at least 21 years old and to have held a license for a year or more; larger vehicles, vans, and luxury cars often bump the minimum age up to around 26, and drivers aged 21–25 may be charged a young-driver surcharge.

Expect to pay roughly 50,000–110,000 KRW a day for a compact car, plus 10,000–40,000 KRW a day for insurance (CDW). It's worth paying extra for the "zero-deductible" or "Super CDW" option if it's offered — without it, you could be on the hook for a large repair bill after even a small accident. Airport pickup is often a little cheaper than picking up in central Seoul. Prices and exact IDP rules can vary by company and change over time, so double-check both when you book.

Driving Rules Foreigners Often Get Wrong

Korea drives on the right-hand side of the road, with the steering wheel on the left — the same setup as the US, Canada, and most of mainland Europe, so it'll feel familiar if you're coming from one of those countries. If you're used to right-hand-drive cars (UK, Japan, Australia, etc.), give yourself a few extra minutes to adjust before pulling out of the rental lot.

The rule that catches the most visitors out: since 2023, you must come to a complete stop before turning right on a red light — even if the road looks completely clear. Rolling through at a slow speed can still get you a ticket (around 60,000 KRW). Turning right is also not allowed at all where a separate right-turn signal controls that lane.

Speed cameras, both fixed and mobile, are everywhere, and speed limits are strictly enforced — typically around 100–110 km/h on expressways and much lower on regular roads. Pay extra attention near schools: "child protection zones" usually cap speeds at 30 km/h, and fines there are higher than normal. Koreans themselves tend to slow down noticeably in these zones for exactly that reason — it's one of the few speed limits almost nobody tries to push.


A typical Seoul intersection — exactly the kind of spot where the full-stop-before-right-turn rule gets enforced. Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Tolls, Hi-Pass, and Finding Your Way Without Google Maps

Korea's expressways are tolled, and most lanes use Hi-Pass, an electronic toll system that lets cars pass through without stopping. Ask your rental company whether the car already has a Hi-Pass unit installed and whether tolls get billed to your card automatically when you return the car — policies differ by company. If you're not sure your car is set up for it, stay out of the lane marked for Hi-Pass only (usually on the far left, marked with purple signage) and use a regular toll lane instead, since driving through a Hi-Pass lane without a working unit can trigger a violation notice.

One thing that surprises a lot of visitors: Google Maps doesn't give turn-by-turn driving directions inside Korea, because of local map-data export rules. Use Naver Map or Kakao Map instead — both have English-language modes, voice-guided navigation, and decent English place-name search, and they're what locals actually use for driving directions too, not just foreigners.

Gas stations (주유소, "juyuso") are increasingly self-service — you pump your own fuel and pay by card at the pump or a machine. If you prefer, full-service stations with staff pumping for you still exist and aren't hard to find, especially outside big cities.


A tollgate on a Korean expressway. Photo: Hankook12, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Rental Car vs. Train, Bus, or Taxi: Which Should You Pick?

Renting a car isn't the right call for every trip. If you're only visiting Seoul and a couple of nearby cities, trains and buses will almost always be cheaper and less stressful. A rental car earns its cost when you want to stop at small, hard-to-reach places on your own schedule — think Jeju's coastline, rural temples, or a multi-stop countryside itinerary.

Option Cost Flexibility Best for
Rental car ~60,000–150,000 KRW/day (car + insurance) Highest — go anywhere, anytime Jeju, coastal routes, rural areas with few buses
KTX / train From ~10,000–60,000 KRW per trip Fixed schedules, but very fast City-to-city travel (Seoul–Busan, etc.)
Intercity bus Usually cheaper than KTX More routes than trains, slower Smaller towns without a train station
Taxi Highest for long distances Door-to-door, no driving required Short trips, late nights, zero paperwork

meta_description: A beginner's guide to renting a car in Korea: the IDP you need, rental costs, Hi-Pass tolls, right-turn-on-red rules, and which map app to use.
